title: Acute Care Foundations
description: A starter curriculum of synthetic acute-care reasoning cases, viva prompts, OSCE stations and retrieval questions. Designed for formative practice and educator review.
intended_use: Clinical education only; not a patient-care protocol or a substitute for local guidance.

generation_policy.seeded_variation: question option order only; clinical facts remain fixed

units.title: Acute chest pain: risk-aware first assessment
objectives: Structure a chest-pain history around onset, character, radiation, duration and associated symptoms.
Identify features that require urgent escalation under the local acute chest-pain pathway.
Explain why symptom response to a medicine should not be used alone to establish a diagnosis.

case.presentation: Intermittent central chest discomfort over the last hour, now recurring at rest.
case.history: The learner has not yet established radiation, associated symptoms, cardiovascular history or risk factors.
case.observations: BP 146/88 mmHg; pulse 104/min; respiratory rate 20/min; SpO₂ 96% on room air; temperature 36.8 °C. These values are fictional teaching data.
revealed_findings: The discomfort radiates to the left arm.
The patient reports nausea and sweating.
The patient has a history of hypertension and smoking.
case.task: Take a focused history, identify urgency, select appropriate initial assessment steps and communicate the concern. Do not delay an indicated emergency pathway for completion of the exercise.

teaching_points: Describe pain characteristics precisely rather than recording only 'chest pain'.
Consider associated symptoms and haemodynamic status alongside risk factors.
A normal or unavailable early test does not replace clinical assessment.
Use the local acute coronary syndrome pathway when suspicion is present.
pitfalls: Assuming that all acute coronary syndromes present with central pain alone.
Using response to glyceryl trinitrate as a diagnostic test.
Allowing non-essential investigations to delay an indicated transfer or escalation.

quiz.stem: Which missing history element most directly improves the initial characterisation of this pain?
options: Onset, duration, radiation and provoking or relieving factors
The patient's preferred pharmacy
The exact time of the last routine dental visit
A complete dietary diary for the previous month
quiz.rationale: A structured pain history records onset, duration, site, radiation, severity and provoking or relieving factors, alongside associated symptoms and relevant cardiovascular history.

quiz.stem: The patient says the discomfort improved after a nitrate. What is the safest interpretation?
options: This response alone confirms a coronary diagnosis
This response alone excludes a coronary diagnosis
The response is not sufficiently specific to establish the diagnosis
The response makes further assessment unnecessary
quiz.rationale: NICE advises not to use response to glyceryl trinitrate to make the diagnosis. Integrate the history, examination, ECG, biomarkers and appropriate pathway.

quiz.stem: Which accompanying feature should increase concern in this vignette?
options: Chest discomfort associated with sweating and nausea
A remote uncomplicated ankle sprain
A preference for sitting near a window
A normal appetite yesterday
quiz.rationale: Associated autonomic symptoms such as sweating and nausea can increase concern in the context of suspected acute coronary syndrome; interpret them with the whole presentation.

viva.prompt: How would you distinguish a focused chest-pain history from a generic symptom list?
key_points: Haemodynamic symptoms and dangerous alternative diagnoses

viva.prompt: Why should a response to symptom-relief medication not be used as a diagnostic shortcut?
key_points: Treatment response is not sufficiently specific
Risk of false reassurance or anchoring
Need for objective assessment and pathway-based evaluation

osce.title: Focused assessment of acute chest pain
osce.candidate_instructions: You have 7 minutes to take a focused history, identify immediate concerns and explain the initial assessment and escalation plan. This is a communication and reasoning station, not a prescribing station.
checklist: Establishes onset, duration, site, character and severity
Asks about radiation and associated symptoms
Elicits relevant cardiovascular history and risk factors
Checks current symptoms and features of instability
Identifies need for appropriate urgent pathway when indicated
Summarises uncertainty and communicates a clear plan
critical_errors: Uses response to nitrate as proof of diagnosis
Provides false reassurance despite concerning ongoing symptoms
Delays indicated escalation for non-essential tasks

debrief: Which feature most changed your level of concern?
What information remained unknown at the point of your decision?
Did you communicate urgency without overstating diagnostic certainty?

units.title: Acute asthma: assess, treat and reassess
objectives: Describe a structured assessment of an acute asthma presentation.
Use objective airflow information when available and appropriate.
Reassess clinical response and recognise when escalation is required.

case.presentation: Worsening breathlessness and wheeze over several hours after a respiratory illness.
case.history: The patient reports increasing reliever use. Previous asthma history and current preventer use need clarification.
case.observations: Pulse 108/min; respiratory rate 24/min; SpO₂ 94% on room air; temperature 37.2 °C. Fictional values for learning only.
revealed_findings: The patient is speaking in short phrases.
Peak expiratory flow is pending until measured in the scenario.
After an intervention, the learner must reassess symptoms, work of breathing and objective measures when available.
case.task: Complete a focused assessment, identify severity concerns, select actions within the locally approved pathway and reassess the response.

teaching_points: Assess speech, work of breathing, respiratory observations and overall appearance.
Ask about previous severe attacks, recent treatment and medication use.
Use objective airflow measurement when appropriate and do not let measurement delay urgent escalation.
Document response to treatment and reassessment, not merely the treatment given.
pitfalls: Treating one observation as a complete severity assessment.
Failing to reassess after intervention.
Assuming improvement in one measure proves full recovery.
Using a teaching scenario as a substitute for local asthma protocols.

quiz.stem: Which combination best reflects a structured reassessment after an intervention?
options: Symptoms, speech, work of breathing, observations and objective airflow when available
Only the patient's age
Only whether the prescribed intervention was recorded
Only the initial oxygen saturation
quiz.rationale: Reassessment should consider the patient's clinical state and relevant objective measures. A recorded intervention is not evidence of response.

quiz.stem: A patient appears exhausted and is becoming less able to speak. What is the educational priority?
options: Continue routine history-taking before escalation
Recognise potential deterioration and activate the appropriate urgent pathway
Wait for every investigation to return
Assume wheeze intensity alone determines severity
quiz.rationale: Signs of exhaustion or worsening ability to speak are concerning. Escalation must follow the current local emergency pathway; investigations must not delay necessary action.

quiz.stem: Why is documenting a post-intervention assessment important?
options: It proves the intervention was correct in every case
It records whether the clinical state changed and supports the next decision
It replaces the need for monitoring
It removes the need to record uncertainty
quiz.rationale: The response and remaining uncertainty inform subsequent decisions. Documentation should make the sequence and rationale visible.

viva.prompt: What information would you seek before deciding how urgently to escalate an acute asthma presentation?
key_points: Work of breathing and general appearance
Previous severe episodes and current treatment
Objective airflow when appropriate and without delaying urgent care

viva.prompt: What would you include in a meaningful reassessment?
key_points: Repeat observations and objective measures when indicated

osce.title: Acute asthma assessment and reassessment
osce.candidate_instructions: Perform a focused assessment on a simulated adult with worsening breathlessness. State when urgent help is required and describe how you would reassess after an intervention.
checklist: Assesses speech and general appearance
Assesses work of breathing
Reviews vital observations
Asks about prior severe attacks and recent treatment
Identifies appropriate objective airflow assessment when feasible
States escalation triggers
Documents and reassesses response
critical_errors: Delays urgent escalation to complete routine measurements
Does not reassess after intervention
Treats a single normal observation as proof of recovery

debrief: Which finding most influenced your assessment of severity?
What did you know before acting, and what remained unknown?
How did the reassessment change your next-step reasoning?

units.title: Suspected sepsis: recognise risk and communicate
objectives: Recognise that suspected infection may present with non-specific features.
Integrate observations, clinical concern and vulnerability rather than relying on fever alone.
Communicate deterioration and reassessment needs clearly.

case.presentation: A patient with a two-day history of feeling unwell, reduced oral intake and new confusion.
case.history: The source of infection is not yet clear. A family member reports a noticeable change from baseline behaviour.
case.observations: Temperature 37.1 °C; pulse 116/min; respiratory rate 24/min; blood pressure 96/62 mmHg; SpO₂ 95% on room air. Fictional values; do not calculate or infer a formal score from this vignette.
revealed_findings: The patient has reduced urine output.
The family member reports worsening function over the previous day.
The likely source remains uncertain.
case.task: Recognise concern, gather missing information, communicate promptly and use the current local sepsis pathway. Do not independently prescribe from this educational unit.

teaching_points: Sepsis should be considered when infection is possible and the person is seriously unwell, even without a high temperature.
Listen to the patient, family and carers about change from baseline.
Use the current local risk-assessment and escalation framework.
Reassess when the patient deteriorates or does not improve.
pitfalls: Excluding sepsis because the temperature is not high.
Ignoring family observations or communication barriers.
Treating a score as a substitute for clinical judgement.
Failing to reassess after an initial plan.

quiz.stem: Which feature should prevent false reassurance from the temperature reading?
options: The patient is afebrile but has confusion, tachycardia and low blood pressure
The patient is wearing a blue shirt
The patient reports a remote healed fracture
The patient prefers written information
quiz.rationale: Suspected sepsis can present without a high temperature. Interpret the whole clinical picture, vulnerability and concern.

quiz.stem: A family member reports that the patient's behaviour is markedly different from baseline. How should this information be handled?
options: Ignore it unless the patient repeats it
Record it as collateral history and incorporate it into assessment
Treat it as a confirmed infection source
Use it to replace observations
quiz.rationale: Collateral information about changes from usual behaviour can be important, especially when the patient has difficulty providing a history.

quiz.stem: The patient's condition worsens after the initial assessment. What is the best learning response?
options: Keep the original plan unchanged
Reassess and escalate according to the current local pathway
Wait for the next routine review regardless of condition
Remove the earlier observations from the record
quiz.rationale: Deterioration or failure to improve requires reassessment and escalation in accordance with local guidance.

viva.prompt: Why can a normal temperature fail to exclude serious infection?
key_points: Consider organ dysfunction, perfusion, mental state and trajectory

viva.prompt: How would you incorporate collateral history into an acute assessment?
key_points: Identify the source and time of the information
Use it alongside direct assessment and observations

osce.title: Recognising and escalating suspected sepsis
osce.candidate_instructions: Review the synthetic patient, identify concerning features, obtain relevant collateral history and give a concise escalation handover. Follow local policy for any clinical action.
checklist: Recognises possible infection with systemic concern
Interprets observations as a pattern
Asks about baseline function and change
Obtains collateral history where useful
Identifies need for timely senior review/escalation
States need for reassessment and documentation
critical_errors: Rules out concern solely because temperature is not high
Ignores new confusion or deterioration
Does not escalate despite concerning overall presentation

debrief: Which cue made you concerned despite the absence of fever?
How did collateral history affect your interpretation?
What would trigger earlier reassessment?

units.title: Suspected stroke: establish time and deficit
objectives: Characterise the onset and evolution of a focal neurological deficit.
Establish and communicate last-known-well time.
Recognise the need for immediate activation of the local stroke pathway.

case.presentation: Sudden onset difficulty speaking and weakness of the right arm, first noticed by a colleague.
case.history: The exact onset is not yet known. The colleague can describe when the patient was last seen at their usual baseline.
case.observations: Pulse 92/min; blood pressure 168/94 mmHg; capillary glucose 6.1 mmol/L. Fictional teaching values.
revealed_findings: The colleague last saw the patient at baseline at 08:10.
Symptoms were noticed at 08:45.
The patient takes a regular anticoagulant; the exact medicine and last dose need clarification.
case.task: Identify a time-critical focal deficit, establish last-known-well and key medication history, and activate the local stroke pathway.

teaching_points: Record exact last-known-well time and the source of that information.
Describe the deficit and its evolution.
Check for important mimics and immediate safety issues without delaying a stroke pathway.
Communicate anticoagulant use and relevant medication timing.
pitfalls: Recording discovery time as onset time without qualification.
Failing to identify the collateral source.
Allowing non-essential tests to delay urgent stroke assessment.
Omitting anticoagulant history.

quiz.stem: The symptom was noticed at 08:45, but the patient was last known well at 08:10. Which time should be documented as last-known-well?
options: 08:10, with the source recorded
The time the learner began the examination
An estimated midpoint without explanation
quiz.rationale: Last-known-well is the last time the patient was known to be at their baseline. Record the source and distinguish it from symptom discovery time.

quiz.stem: Which medication detail is especially important to clarify in this vignette?
options: Anticoagulant name and last dose
The brand of toothpaste
The patient's preferred meal
Remote vitamin use without relevance
quiz.rationale: Anticoagulant exposure and timing can materially affect stroke assessment and should be communicated to the treating team.

quiz.stem: What should happen when a sudden focal neurological deficit is suspected?
options: Wait for a routine outpatient appointment
Activate the appropriate local emergency stroke pathway
Complete a full elective history before escalation
Assume symptoms are benign if they fluctuate
quiz.rationale: Suspected stroke is time-critical. Use the regional emergency stroke pathway and do not delay activation for non-essential tasks.

viva.prompt: Why is last-known-well different from the time symptoms were discovered?
key_points: Symptoms may be unwitnessed or discovered later
Time and source need explicit documentation

viva.prompt: What information would you communicate in the first handover?
key_points: Anticoagulant and other relevant medication history

osce.title: Time-critical stroke history and handover
osce.candidate_instructions: Obtain a focused collateral history, identify the deficit and communicate the timeline and relevant medicines to the receiving stroke team.
checklist: Identifies focal neurological symptoms
Establishes last-known-well time
Separates last-known-well from discovery time
Records collateral source
Clarifies anticoagulant use and timing
Activates local stroke pathway promptly
critical_errors: Fails to establish or communicate last-known-well
Delays stroke pathway activation for non-essential tasks
Omits known anticoagulant use

debrief: Which time did you initially record and why?
What source supported the last-known-well time?
What information could have been lost in handover?

units.title: Acute headache: identify secondary red flags
objectives: Characterise headache onset, time to peak and associated symptoms.
Identify features that warrant further investigation or referral.
Avoid premature classification as a primary headache when red flags are present.

case.presentation: A new severe headache that reached maximum intensity rapidly.
case.history: The learner has not yet asked about neurological symptoms, fever, trauma, pregnancy/postpartum status or previous headache pattern.
case.observations: Alert at initial contact; other observations not yet obtained. Fictional scenario.
revealed_findings: The patient describes maximal intensity within minutes.
There is no established history of similar episodes.
The focused neurological assessment has not yet been completed.
case.task: Identify red flags, obtain a focused history and explain why urgent assessment may be required.

teaching_points: Establish whether onset was sudden and how quickly pain reached maximum intensity.
Ask about new neurological symptoms, fever, trauma and relevant context.
A new or substantially changed headache pattern requires careful assessment.
Do not label a headache as primary before considering secondary causes.
pitfalls: Treating severe pain as sufficient to classify a migraine.
Failing to establish time to peak.
Ignoring a new neurological deficit or altered consciousness.
Ordering or omitting imaging without a clinical rationale.

quiz.stem: Which headache feature is a red flag in the NICE guidance?
options: Sudden onset reaching maximum intensity within five minutes
A stable, familiar pattern over many years without change
Mild pain after a long day with no other symptoms
A headache diary entry
quiz.rationale: NICE identifies sudden-onset headache reaching maximum intensity within five minutes as a feature that warrants evaluation for further investigation or referral.

quiz.stem: What is the most important next history clarification in this vignette?
options: Time from onset to maximum intensity and associated neurological or systemic symptoms
The patient's favourite exercise
The exact brand of their mobile phone
Their usual breakfast choices
quiz.rationale: The time course and associated red flags help distinguish a potentially secondary headache from a familiar primary pattern.

quiz.stem: A patient with a new headache reports a new focal neurological deficit. What should the learner do?
options: Assume uncomplicated migraine without further assessment
Recognise a red flag and follow the urgent local assessment pathway
Recommend only a routine headache diary
Wait for symptoms to resolve before documenting
quiz.rationale: A new neurological deficit is a red flag in headache assessment and requires appropriate further evaluation.

viva.prompt: How do you distinguish a familiar primary headache pattern from a potentially secondary headache?
Why is premature diagnostic labelling dangerous in a new severe headache?
key_points: Requires documented red-flag assessment and uncertainty

osce.title: Focused headache history with red-flag screen
osce.candidate_instructions: Take a focused headache history and explain which features would change the urgency of assessment. Do not provide an unsupported diagnosis.
checklist: Establishes onset and progression
Asks time to maximum intensity
Asks about neurological symptoms and consciousness
Asks about fever and recent trauma
Clarifies previous pattern and relevant context
Explains escalation if red flags are present
critical_errors: Ignores sudden maximal-at-onset headache
Ignores a new focal neurological deficit
Provides definitive reassurance without adequate assessment

debrief: Which question most changed your differential?
Did you establish time to peak precisely?
What uncertainty remains after the first assessment?

units.title: Transient loss of consciousness: reconstruct the event
objectives: Reconstruct the event using patient and witness accounts.
Identify features that raise concern for a cardiac cause or another serious diagnosis.
Recognise the role of ECG and focused assessment.

case.presentation: A brief episode of collapse while walking uphill, with rapid recovery.
case.history: The patient is unsure of the duration. A witness saw the event but has not yet been interviewed.
case.observations: Currently alert; pulse 88/min; blood pressure 124/78 mmHg. Fictional values.
revealed_findings: The witness reports no prolonged confusion after the episode.
The patient remembers palpitations immediately before collapse.
A first-degree relative died suddenly at a young age.
case.task: Obtain the witness account, characterise the event and identify the need for appropriate cardiovascular assessment.

teaching_points: Ask about posture, activity, prodrome, colour, movements, duration and recovery.
Witness accounts can clarify event sequence and recovery.
Consider exertional collapse, palpitations and family history of sudden death as concerning features.
ECG is an important part of the initial assessment.
pitfalls: Assuming every collapse is a seizure or simple faint.
Ignoring exertional onset or palpitations.
Failing to obtain a witness account.
Not documenting recovery and post-event confusion.

quiz.stem: Which detail most increases concern for a cardiac cause in this vignette?
options: Collapse during exertion with preceding palpitations
A remote uncomplicated skin rash
Feeling hungry before lunch
A preference for sleeping on one side
quiz.rationale: Exertional syncope and palpitations are important red flags and warrant appropriate cardiovascular assessment.

quiz.stem: Why is a witness account valuable?
options: It replaces the patient's history in every case
It can clarify event duration, observed movements and recovery
It confirms a diagnosis without examination
It is only useful when the patient is unconscious now
quiz.rationale: A witness can provide important details of the event and recovery, particularly when the patient has incomplete recall.

quiz.stem: Which test is a core part of initial assessment for transient loss of consciousness in NICE guidance?
options: 12-lead ECG
Routine whole-body CT for every patient
A screening chest MRI
No investigations are required
quiz.rationale: A 12-lead ECG is part of the initial assessment and can reveal abnormalities that require further evaluation.

viva.prompt: What event details help distinguish syncope from other causes of transient loss of consciousness?
Which historical features should prompt concern for a cardiac cause?
key_points: Family history of sudden cardiac death
Known structural heart disease or abnormal ECG

osce.title: Witness-informed assessment after collapse
osce.candidate_instructions: Take a focused history from the patient and witness, then summarise features that affect urgency and the need for ECG-based assessment.
checklist: Establishes circumstances and posture
Asks about prodrome and palpitations
Obtains witness description
Clarifies duration and recovery
Asks about family history and cardiac history
Identifies ECG and appropriate referral considerations
critical_errors: Ignores exertional collapse
Ignores preceding palpitations or family sudden death
Fails to obtain witness details when available

debrief: What did the witness add that the patient could not?
Which red flag most affected your next step?
How did you distinguish event description from diagnostic conclusion?

units.title: Meningitis: recognise a dangerous combination
objectives: Recognise a concerning combination of fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered cognition.
Understand that absence of one feature does not automatically exclude meningitis.
Communicate suspected meningitis and the need for emergency assessment.

case.presentation: Fever, severe headache and increasing drowsiness over the day.
case.history: The learner has not yet clarified neck stiffness, rash, exposure history or recent change in cognition.
case.observations: Temperature 39.0 °C; pulse 122/min; respiratory rate 23/min. Fictional values.
revealed_findings: The patient reports neck pain and photophobia.
A friend reports that the patient is unusually confused.
No rash is visible at the first examination.
case.task: Recognise the concern, communicate promptly and activate the local emergency transfer pathway when meningitis is suspected.

teaching_points: A combination of fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered consciousness or cognition is a major red-flag pattern.
Clinical suspicion may remain high even when not every feature is present.
A rash is not required before taking a concerning presentation seriously.
Emergency transfer and senior assessment must follow the current local pathway.
pitfalls: Waiting for all classic features before escalating.
Using absence of rash as reassurance.
Allowing non-essential tasks to delay emergency transfer.
Failing to tell the receiving team why meningitis is suspected.

quiz.stem: Which combination is identified by NICE as a major red-flag combination for bacterial meningitis?
options: Fever, headache, neck stiffness and altered consciousness or cognition
Cough, ankle swelling, itch and constipation
Back pain, reflux, rash and insomnia
Headache alone in a person with a long stable history
quiz.rationale: NICE identifies this combination as a strong reason to suspect bacterial meningitis. It is not the only possible presentation.

quiz.stem: The patient has no visible rash. What should the learner conclude?
options: Meningitis is excluded
The absence of rash does not exclude meningitis; interpret the full clinical picture
No further assessment is needed
The patient can automatically be discharged
quiz.rationale: A rash is not required for meningitis to be suspected. Use the overall clinical presentation and local emergency pathway.

quiz.stem: When bacterial meningitis is suspected, what is the appropriate educational priority?
options: Arrange routine follow-up next month
Activate the local emergency transfer and senior assessment pathway
Wait for every investigation before communicating concern
Provide reassurance based on age alone
quiz.rationale: NICE recommends emergency transfer for suspected bacterial meningitis or meningococcal disease. Local protocols govern the operational steps.

viva.prompt: Why should the learner not wait for the complete red-flag combination before considering meningitis?
key_points: Not every feature is present in every person
Need for clinical judgement and full assessment

viva.prompt: What should be included in the emergency handover?

osce.title: Recognising and escalating suspected meningitis
osce.candidate_instructions: Review the synthetic presentation, identify the concerning pattern and give a concise emergency handover. Do not delay escalation to complete routine tasks.
checklist: Recognises fever and severe headache
Asks about neck stiffness and cognition
Obtains collateral history when confusion is present
Does not rely on rash being present
Identifies need for emergency transfer
Communicates concern and key findings clearly
critical_errors: Rules out meningitis because rash is absent
Waits for every feature before escalating
Fails to communicate altered cognition

debrief: Which information changed the level of concern?
What was absent, and why did that not provide reassurance?
Was the urgency clear in your handover?

units.title: Acute abdominal pain: structure the assessment
objectives: Characterise abdominal pain by site, onset, progression and associated symptoms.
Identify peritonism, haemodynamic compromise and other urgent features.
Include pregnancy possibility and relevant surgical history when applicable.

case.presentation: Progressive lower abdominal pain with nausea.
case.history: The learner has not yet established exact onset, migration, bowel and urinary symptoms, menstrual history or pregnancy possibility.
case.observations: Pulse 108/min; blood pressure 112/72 mmHg; temperature 37.8 °C. Fictional values.
revealed_findings: Pain has localised to the right lower abdomen.
Movement worsens the pain.
Pregnancy possibility has not yet been established.
case.task: Take a structured history, identify urgent features and explain a proportionate investigation strategy using local pathways.

teaching_points: Record location, onset, character, radiation and progression.
Ask about vomiting, bowel, urinary and reproductive symptoms where relevant.
Consider pregnancy possibility where clinically applicable.
Look for peritonism and haemodynamic compromise.
Use serial examination when the diagnosis remains uncertain.
pitfalls: Anchoring on one diagnosis before exploring alternatives.
Failing to consider pregnancy possibility when relevant.
Ignoring pain progression or peritoneal features.
Treating a single reassuring observation as definitive.

quiz.stem: Which history element is important to include when clinically applicable in an adult with lower abdominal pain?
options: Pregnancy possibility and relevant menstrual/reproductive history
The exact number of daily emails
A complete childhood school record
The patient's preferred television programme
quiz.rationale: Pregnancy possibility and relevant reproductive history can materially change the differential diagnosis and investigation strategy.

quiz.stem: The pain is becoming localised and movement worsens it. What should the learner do?
options: Document progression and assess for peritoneal features and instability
Assume it is benign because nausea is present
Avoid examination
Wait for the pain to resolve without reassessment
quiz.rationale: Progression, localisation and movement-related pain should prompt focused assessment, including urgent features and serial review when needed.

quiz.stem: The initial diagnosis remains uncertain after the first assessment. What is a defensible approach?
options: Record uncertainty, reassess and use targeted investigations based on the evolving picture
Invent a definitive diagnosis to complete the form
Repeat every possible investigation without a question
Delete the initial assessment
quiz.rationale: Clinical reasoning should preserve uncertainty and use evolving findings to guide targeted investigation and reassessment.

viva.prompt: How would you structure the history of acute abdominal pain?
key_points: Onset, site, character, radiation, severity and progression
Associated gastrointestinal, urinary and reproductive symptoms

viva.prompt: What findings would change the urgency of assessment?
key_points: Bleeding, pregnancy-related concerns or other time-critical features

osce.title: Structured history for acute abdominal pain
osce.candidate_instructions: Take a focused history, identify important missing information and explain what findings would trigger urgent escalation.
checklist: Characterises pain and its progression
Asks relevant gastrointestinal and urinary symptoms
Asks reproductive/pregnancy history when applicable
Reviews previous surgery and medicines
Assesses for instability and peritoneal features
States uncertainty and a targeted plan
critical_errors: Fails to consider pregnancy when relevant
Ignores signs of peritonism or instability
Gives definitive reassurance without adequate assessment

debrief: What was your first anchor and did you test alternatives?
Which missing history item could change the pathway?
How did you handle diagnostic uncertainty?
